questions.question_text: Voucherbased contingency clinical approach has been found to have the best outcome in individuals with which of the following substance use disorders?

options.text: A diagnosis of cocaine use disorder
A diagnosis of alcohol use disorder
A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder
A diagnosis of tobacco use disorder
A diagnosis of opioid use disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of cocaine use disorder

questions.explanation: Several psychosocial therapies have been studied in cocaine use disorder, including 12step facilitation, 192 • PSYCHIATRY cognitive behavioral therapy, and contingency management. Voucherbased contingency management has yielded better outcomes in a number of studies in patients with cocaine use disorder. Patients with cocaine use disorder tend to score high on reward dependence, which is thought to mediate a portion of the effectiveness of contingency management. Re FeRe NCeS Budney, A. J., & Higgins, S. T. (1990). A community reinforcement plus vouchers approach: Treating cocaine addiction. Rockville, MD: National Institute on Drug Abuse. Petry, N. M., Tedford, J., Austin, M., Nich, C., Carroll, K. M., & Rounsaville, B. J. (2004). Prize reinforcement contingency management for treating cocaine users: How low can we go, and with whom? Addiction, 99, 349–

questions.question_text: A patient experiences feelings of attraction toward their therapist after a session, then goes to the gym and works out vigorously. Which defense mechanism is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is the redirection of emotional energy (feelings of attraction) into socially acceptable activities (vigorous exercise), which is what occurred in this scenario.

questions.question_text: In Freud's model of mourning, the individual's life force must be fully withdrawn from attachment to the deceased person through a process called:
questions.explanation: Freud's model of mourning describes decathexis, the process by which an individual's life force must be fully withdrawn from its attachment to the deceased person.

questions.question_text: In systemic family therapy (Milan approach), the therapist emphasizes which of the following?

options.text: Reflection and circular questioning about family relationships

correct_answer.text: Reflection and circular questioning about family relationships

questions.explanation: The Milan systemic (structural) approach uses circular questioning and reflecting to explore family interaction patterns and relationships.

questions.question_text: Which factor is the best predictor of suitability for psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: Absence of psychotic illness, substance use disorder, or organic illness
Ego strength to address both past and present issues simultaneously

correct_answer.text: Ego strength to address both past and present issues simultaneously

questions.explanation: Good ego strength—the capacity to reflect on past and present emotional experiences and tolerate the therapeutic process—is the strongest predictor of benefit from psychodynamic psychotherapy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a Kleinian defense mechanism?
questions.explanation: Isolation is not a Kleinian defense mechanism. It involves creation of a gap between unpleasant cognitions and other thoughts. Kleinian defenses (SIPDOG) include Splitting, Introjection, Projection, Projective Identification, Denial, Omnipotence, and Grandiosity.

questions.question_text: CAT - Snags, Dilemmas, Traps A therapist identifies patterns where the patient sabotages success, faces impossible choices, or gets stuck in self-reinforcing cycles. Which therapy uses these concepts?
questions.explanation: CAT (Cognitive Analytic Therapy) uses snags (self-sabotage), dilemmas (false either/or choices), and traps (self-reinforcing patterns).

questions.question_text: Circular causality in family systems theory suggests:

options.text: Mutual, reciprocal causality among family members
One member is responsible for all problems
Problems are external to the family

correct_answer.text: Mutual, reciprocal causality among family members

questions.explanation: Circular causality in family systems theory describes mutual, reciprocal causality where family members' behaviors influence each other in circular patterns.

questions.question_text: Which family therapy approach emphasizes hierarchy, boundaries, and structural reorganization?
questions.explanation: Structural family therapy, developed by Salvador Minuchin, emphasizes clear hierarchies, appropriate boundaries, and restructuring dysfunctional family patterns.

questions.question_text: Which psychotherapy approach incorporates Beck's analytic therapy into Rogerian theory?
questions.explanation: Cognitive therapy, developed by Albert Beck, incorporates analytic concepts while maintaining a structured, goal-oriented approach. When combined with Rogerian principles, it represents the integration of Beck's cognitive techniques with person-centered therapeutic elements.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the approach that reflects on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviours?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is a counselling method that helps people resolve ambivalent feelings and insecurities to find the internal motivation they need to change their behaviour. It is a practical, empathetic, and short-term process that takes into consideration how difficult it is to make life changes.

questions.question_text: Among the options below, which one psychotherapeutic modalities is most effective for substance use disorder?
questions.explanation: Although some of these psychotherapeutic modalities are used in patients with substance use disorders, the most effective modality is motivational interviewing. Re FeRe NCeS Miller, W. R., & Rollnick, S. (2012). Motivational interviewing: Helping people change. New York: Guilford Press. Work Group on Substance Use Disorders. (2006). American Psychiatric Association practice guideline for the treatment of patients with substance use disorders (2nd ed., p. 40). Retrieved from http:// psychiatryonline.org/ guidelines

questions.question_text: Habit reversal components include all the following with the exception of

options.text: Development of awareness of the behavior and its triggers
Practice of an incompatible alternative behavior

questions.explanation: Habit reversal is a complex procedure used generally to treat tics, Tourette’s syndrome and stuttering. The treatment has fi ve components – training in becoming aware of the onset of the behaviour; monitoring the behaviour; training in initiating competing responses that are compatible with the behaviour; relaxation; and social support. Training in thought stopping is not a component of habit reversal training. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 593.

questions.question_text: Which treatment approach for panic disorder is described as both an alternative and an augmentation to pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural psychotherapy is described as both an alternative or an augmentation to psychopharmacological approaches in panic disorder. It helps modify cognitive distortions about the catastrophic meaning of panic symptoms, and through graduated exposure techniques, diminishes phobic avoidance behaviours. This dual role — as standalone treatment or combination with medication — reflects the evidence that psychotherapy for anxiety disorders can sometimes be as effective as or more effective than pharmacotherapy alone.

questions.question_text: Orgasmic reconditioning is used in
questions.explanation: Orgasmic reconditioning was fi rst described by Marquis in 1970. In this treatment, the individual is asked to masturbate regularly to their troublesome deviant fantasies, but at the point of orgasmic inevitability, to switch to a desired non-deviant fantasy. As treatment progresses, the non-deviant stimulus is introduced earlier and earlier in the arousal process until masturbation is achieved without the deviant fantasy. This technique obviously is used when the behaviour or sexual preference that is of concern is not in itself dangerous or causing a public nuisance. Following the treatment, further sexual and social skills training is usually needed to ensure that the arousal to non-deviant stimuli is maintained. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 165.

questions.question_text: Detouring in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Redirecting family conflict through a child

correct_answer.text: Redirecting family conflict through a child

questions.explanation: Detouring is a family dynamic where parents redirect their marital conflict through a child, often by coalitioning with the child against the other parent.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a Kleinian defence?
questions.explanation: Isolation is not a Kleinian defence. It is characterized as a mental process involving the creation of a gap between an unpleasant or threatening cognition and other thoughts and feelings. The other defences listed (projective identification, splitting, introjection, and denial) are more primitive Kleinian defences addressed in her work with children.

questions.question_text: In dynamic psychotherapy, the therapist at times uses certain techniques that represent the ‘supportive’ end of the psychodynamic continuum rather than the ‘expressive’ end. Which of the following is suggestive of a ‘supportive’ technique?

options.text: Validation of the individual's emotional experience

questions.explanation: Dynamic (psychoanalytic) psychotherapy is often conceptualised as being on a continuum of expressive to supportive. Traditionally, psychoanalytic psychotherapy has focused on the recovery of repressed psychological material. This process has been called ‘expressive’ and is distinguished from the ‘supportive’ psychotherapies, which concentrate on supporting healthy defence (coping) mechanisms. The therapist may employ more or less expressive and supportive interventions, depending on the needs of the patient. Among the given responses in the question, advice giving leans towards the supportive end of the continuum. In addition to advice giving, other techniques usually employed that are at the supportive end of the continuum are praise, suggestions, reassurance, environmental intervention, and manipulation. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 928. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. (). Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1852.

questions.question_text: Cognitive behavioural therapy using exposure techniques may work by facilitating fear extinction through which mechanism?

options.text: Blocking NMDA receptor activation during exposure to prevent re-conditioning
Increasing serotonergic tone in the amygdala via stress-induced neuroplasticity
Requiring the patient to confront feared stimuli in a safe environment, triggering extinction learning in the amygdala
Reducing noradrenergic output from the locus coeruleus through relaxation training
Strengthening VMPFC-to-thalamus connectivity, bypassing the amygdala entirely

correct_answer.text: Requiring the patient to confront feared stimuli in a safe environment, triggering extinction learning in the amygdala

questions.explanation: Exposure-based CBT is hypothetically effective because it confronts patients with feared stimuli in a safe therapeutic environment without adverse consequences. Repeated safe exposure triggers the process of fear extinction in the amygdala — the VMPFC and hippocampus learn a new, safe context for the feared stimulus and establish new inhibitory connections in the amygdala. The limitation is that this learning is often context-specific, explaining why benefits may not fully generalise to real-world environments.

questions.question_text: A patient becomes angry at their therapist, saying 'Where were you when I was young and needed help?' What psychodynamic concept does this represent?
questions.explanation: Transference involves redirecting feelings about significant others (such as parents) onto the therapist. The patient is relating to the therapist as a parental figure.

questions.question_text: The belief \'I am worthless\' is an example of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Core maladaptive schemas are deep, enduring cognitive structures — typically unconditional beliefs about the self beginning with \'I am…\' (e.g., \'I am unlovable\') — that develop through early experiences and perpetuate dysphoric mood and self-defeating behaviour (Beck et al., 1979). They are distinguished from conditional assumptions (\'I must…\'/\'I should…\') and surface-level automatic thoughts. The stem example (\'I must be perfect to be accepted\') is technically a conditional assumption, but in the absence of that option, maladaptive schema (C) is the best fit because it is a deeper, enduring dysfunctional belief rather than a transient automatic thought (A), a logical processing error/cognitive error (D), or the specific distortion of personalization (E). Adaptive schema (B) is incorrect because the belief is clearly dysfunctional.

questions.question_text: Openended questions, affirmations, reflective statements, and summary statements (OARS) are the central components of which of the following therapeutic modalities used in the treatment of substance use disorder?
questions.explanation: Some of these techniques are used in a variety of psychotherapeutic treatment modalities, but together they constitute the four essential techniques of motivational enhancement therapy commonly administered in the setting of substance use disorder. Re FeRe NCe Miller, W. R., & Rollnick, S. (2012). Motivational interviewing: Helping people change. New York, NY: Guilford Press.

questions.question_text: Which form of therapy explores how personal stories and cultural narratives shape identity and emphasizes re-authoring life stories toward healthier outcomes?
questions.explanation: Narrative therapy focuses on how personal stories and cultural narratives shape identity and emphasizes re-authoring life stories toward healthier outcomes, particularly in addressing social discourse and meaning-making.

questions.question_text: Mentalization is best defined as which of the following?

options.text: The ability to understand mental states underlying behavior
Lack of concern for others' thoughts

correct_answer.text: The ability to understand mental states underlying behavior

questions.explanation: Mentalization is the ability to understand the mental state—of oneself or others—that underlies overt behavior, allowing perception and interpretation of human behavior in terms of intentional mental states.

questions.question_text: Which therapy is based on the principle of reciprocal inhibition?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization is based on the principle of reciprocal inhibition, where an incompatible relaxation response is paired with anxiety-provoking stimuli.

questions.question_text: Jack is a 35-year-old man who perceived his parents as overly authoritarian. His therapist on the other hand, is friendly and non-authoritarian, but at times fi rm and sets defi nite limits. The attitude of his therapist gave Jack the opportunity to identify with a new parent fi gure. This is an example of a process described by Franz Alexander. Which of the following terms best represents this process?
questions.explanation: The therapeutic relationship between therapist and patient gives a therapist an opportunity to display behaviour different from the destructive or unproductive behaviour of a patient’s parent. At times, such experiences seem to neutralize or reverse some effects of the parents’ mistakes. If the patient had overly authoritarian parents, the therapist’s friendly, fl exible, non-judgemental, non-authoritarian, but at times fi rm and limit-setting attitude gives the patient an opportunity to adjust to, be led by, and identify with a new parent fi gure. Franz Alexander described this process as a corrective emotional experience. It draws on elements of both psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 931.

questions.question_text: A woman comes to your outpatient clinic. She has recurrent thoughts of contamination with germs and has to wash her hands up to 20 times every time she touches wooden surfaces. This prevents her from looking after her 2-year-old child. She is worried that the child may not be gaining the required weight. She has also started to lose the skin of her palms due to the excessive washing. The treatment you would recommend would be

options.text: Combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and CBT

correct_answer.text: Combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and CBT

questions.explanation: According to NICE guidelines, in the initial treatment of adults with OCD, low-intensity psychological treatments (including exposure and response prevention (ERP)) (up to 10 therapist hours per patient) should be offered if the patient’s degree of functional impairment is mild and/ or the patient expresses a preference for a low-intensity approach. These include brief individual CBT (including ERP) using structured self-help materials; brief individual CBT (including ERP) by telephone; group CBT (including ERP) (note, the patient may receive more than 10 hours of therapy in this format). Those with mild functional impairment who are unable to engage in low intensity CBT (including ERP), or for whom low-intensity treatment has proved to be inadequate, should be offered the choice of either a course of an SSRI or more intensive CBT (including ERP) (more than 10 therapist hours per patient). Adults with OCD with moderate functional impairment should be offered the choice of either a course of an SSRI or more intensive CBT (including ERP) (more than 10 therapist hours per patient). Adults with OCD with severe functional impairment should be offered combined treatment with an SSRI and CBT (including ERP). NICE. CG31 Obsessive-compulsive disorder: NICE guideline. Clinical Guidelines (accessed 7 June 7 2009 http://guidance.nice.org.uk/CG31/NiceGuidance/pdf/English).

questions.question_text: In family systems theory, which term describes the process where parents form an alliance against the child to increase closeness in their own relationship, serving as a distraction from marital tension?
questions.explanation: Detouring occurs when parents focus negativity on the child rather than directing anger or criticism toward each other, functioning to create distance between the parents and child while increasing closeness in the marital subsystem. This is also known as scapegoat syndrome.

questions.question_text: What does behavioral activation primarily target?
questions.explanation: Behavioral activation targets avoidance and withdrawal by scheduling pleasurable and meaningful activities. It is particularly effective for depression.

questions.question_text: Reciprocal inhibition is the theoretical basis for which therapeutic technique?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization uses reciprocal inhibition, where anxiety-incompatible responses (relaxation) inhibit fear responses.

questions.question_text: Cognitive analytic therapy is structured into established steps, which the patient moves through over the course of the sessions. Which of the following occurs in the initial sessions of CAT?
questions.explanation: The initial sessions of CAT are devoted to exploration and gathering information about current difficulties and previous experiences, after which the therapist writes a reformulation letter to the patient.

questions.question_text: Being aware that people's interactions are influenced by each other which in turn are influenced by others describes
questions.explanation: Circular causality describes a feedback loop sequence of causes and effects that leads back to the original cause, altering or confirming it. It reflects the systemic understanding that interactions are bidirectionally influential.

questions.question_text: Enmeshment in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Lack of autonomy with blurred boundaries

correct_answer.text: Lack of autonomy with blurred boundaries

questions.explanation: Enmeshment is a family systems concept describing relationships with excessively diffused boundaries, little autonomy, and excessive interdependence.

questions.question_text: Brief psychodynamic psychotherapy has been shown NOT to be of benefi t in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Inclusion criteria for brief psychodynamic psychotherapy diagnoses: depression, mild to moderate; anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, social, panic; somatoform disorders; eating disorders; opiate dependence;. Patient characteristics include good object relationships (has had at least one relationship); highly motivated, ‘willing’ patient; narrow symptom/problem focus; interpersonal diffi culties. Exclusion criteria for brief psychodynamic psychotherapy include a diagnosis of severe depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, suicidality; obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD); severe somatizing disorders; severe eating disorders; poor object relationships; poor motivation; chronic, severe character pathology; diffuse, ill-defi ned symptomatology. Most of the above criteria are derived from a systematic review of psychodynamic psychotherapies by Leichsenring in 2005. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 73. Leichsenring F. (2005). Are psychodynamic and psychoanalytic therapies effective? A review of empirical data. International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 86: 841–868.

questions.question_text: A patient with major depression is being considered for interpersonal therapy (IPT). Which of the following is a component of interpersonal therapy?
questions.explanation: IPT focuses on four key areas: grief, role transitions, interpersonal disputes, and interpersonal deficits.

questions.question_text: A patient with borderline personality disorder begins dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). What is addressed in the first stage of DBT?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 DBT addresses life-threatening behaviors (self-harm, suicidality) first.

questions.question_text: What is mentalization?

options.text: The ability to focus attention on external stimuli
A form of imaginative mental activity that lets us perceive and interpret human behavior in terms of intentional mental states
The process of storing information in long-term memory
The ability to distinguish between reality and fantasy
A defense mechanism involving projection of thoughts onto others

correct_answer.text: A form of imaginative mental activity that lets us perceive and interpret human behavior in terms of intentional mental states

questions.explanation: Mentalization is the ability to understand the mental state of oneself or others that underlies overt behavior, and can be seen as a form of imaginative mental activity that lets us perceive and interpret human behavior in terms of intentional mental states.

questions.question_text: Orgasmic reconditioning is used in
questions.explanation: Orgasmic reconditioning was fi rst described by Marquis in 1970. In this treatment, the individual is asked to masturbate regularly to their troublesome deviant fantasies, but at the point of orgasmic inevitability, to switch to a desired non-deviant fantasy. As treatment progresses, the non-deviant stimulus is introduced earlier and earlier in the arousal process until masturbation is achieved without the deviant fantasy. This technique obviously is used when the behaviour or sexual preference that is of concern is not in itself dangerous or causing a public nuisance. Following the treatment, further sexual and social skills training is usually needed to ensure that the arousal to non-deviant stimuli is maintained. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 165.

questions.question_text: The ability to understand the mental states of oneself or others that underlie overt behaviour is termed:
questions.explanation: Mentalization is the capacity for imaginative mental activity that allows perception and interpretation of human behaviour in terms of intentional mental states such as needs, desires, feelings, beliefs, goals, purposes, and reasons.

questions.question_text: A method of group psychotherapy where members of the group take on the roles of ‘the protagonist’ and ‘auxillary ego’ while the therapist takes on the role of ‘the director’ is
questions.explanation: Psychodrama is a method of group psychotherapy originated by Jacob Moreno, a Viennese-born psychiatrist. In this type of psychotherapy, the personality make-up, interpersonal relationships, confl icts, and emotional problems are explored by means of special ‘dramatic’ methods. Therapeutic dramatization of emotional problems includes the ‘protagonist’ or patient, the person who acts out his/her problems. The enactment is carried out with the help of ‘auxiliary egos’, people who enact varying aspects of the patient. The therapist takes up the role of the ‘director’ and guides those in the drama towards the acquisition of insight. Situations are chosen by the protagonist – this usually focuses on any special area of functioning or symptoms. The auxiliary ego takes on the role of other signifi cant people in the protagonist’s life. The therapist directs the situations, and the group can comment on various ways in which the protagonist deals with the situation he/she is in. Techniques to advance the therapeutic process and to increase productivity and creativity include the soliloquy (a recital of overt and hidden thoughts and feelings), role reversal (the exchange of the patient’s role for the role of a signifi cant person), the double (an auxiliary ego acting as the patient), the multiple double (several egos acting as the patient did on varying occasions), and the mirror technique (an ego imitating the patient and speaking for him or her). Other techniques include the use of hypnosis and psychoactive drugs to modify the acting behaviour in various ways. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 939.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic technique involves imagining a feared situation with maximum intensity to reduce phobic anxiety?
questions.explanation: Implosion therapy (also called implosive therapy) involves having the patient imagine the feared situation with maximum intensity and vividness to reduce phobic anxiety.

questions.question_text: Which theory describes the stages of grief including protest, despair, and detachment?
questions.explanation: Bowlby's attachment and grief theory describes protest, despair, and detachment as stages in the grief and loss response.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach is particularly useful for alcohol addiction by managing triggers
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (cue therapy) focuses on identifying and managing specific cues or triggers that lead to substance cravings and use. This approach is particularly effective in addiction treatment by helping individuals reduce responses to environmental triggers.

questions.question_text: A patient tells their therapist about how wonderful their previous therapist was. Which psychological concept does this represent?
questions.explanation: Idealization/devaluation is a defense mechanism where the patient sees previous figures or aspects of the therapeutic relationship as entirely good (idealization) or entirely bad (devaluation).

questions.question_text: From a psychodynamic perspective, what is thought to underpin obsessive-compulsive disorder?
questions.explanation: Psychodynamic theory views OCD as stemming from unconscious conflicts, with compulsions representing attempts at managing guilt and anxiety through ritual and self-punishment.

questions.question_text: A Rogerian psychotherapy developed by incorporating Beck's analytic therapy is?
questions.explanation: Cognitive therapy combines Rogerian person-centered principles with Beck's cognitive distortion concepts, integrating empathy with structured cognitive techniques.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a principle used during motivational interviewing of substance users?

options.text: Rolling with resistance rather than confronting it directly
Supporting the individual’s sense of self-effi cacy

questions.explanation: Miller and Rollnick (1991) described fi ve principles that are essential to motivational interviewing. They are (1) express empathy: communicate acceptance, use refl ective listening, and normalize a client’s ambivalence; (2) develop discrepancy: increase the client’s awareness of the consequences of the problematic behaviour, orient the client to the discrepancy between his/ her current behaviour and goals in life, and have the client generate reasons for change; (3) avoid argumentation; (4) roll with resistance: invite the client to consider new points of view rather than having them imposed; and (5) support self-effi cacy. O’Donohue WT, Fisher JE and Hayes SC. Cognitive Behavior Therapy: Applying Empirically Supported Techniques in Your Practice. John Wiley & Sons; 2003, p. 252.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach combines Rogers's person-centered methods with Beck's cognitive-behavioral model?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing (MI) and cognitive therapy represent approaches that incorporate Rogers's empathic, client-centered perspective while employing Beck's cognitive-behavioral techniques.

questions.question_text: In the treatment of borderline personality disorder, which of the following does Stage 2 of dialectical behaviour treatment target?

options.text: Maladaptive coping patterns and difficulties with emotional regulation in daily functioning

questions.explanation: Treatment of borderline personality disorder is organized around the level of the disorder, with each level corresponding to one of four stages of treatment with specifi c goals that are targeted towards core defi cits seen in these patients. Stage I: In the fi rst stage of treatment, the therapist seeks to increase behavioural control through helping patients attain basic capacities. This is targeted towards the severe ‘behavioural dyscontrol’ exhibited by the patient. Stage II: The second stage targets ‘quiet desperation’. The intent in this stage is to facilitate emotional experiencing through reducing post-traumatic stress and blocking dissociation. The principal goal of this stage is to block avoidance of emotions and the environmental cues associated with them. In this stage, patients are helped to experience their feelings without avoiding life or experiencing symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. Stage III: The third stage is targeted towards ‘problematic patterns in living’. The goal of this stage is to achieve ‘ordinary happiness and unhappiness’ through increasing self-respect and working on problems with relationships and career choices. Stage IV: The fourth and fi nal stage is directed towards ‘incompleteness’. The goal of the last stage is to develop the patient’s capacity for sustained experience of contentment, connection, and freedom. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 736.

questions.question_text: What is described as the advance made in treating the core symptoms of PTSD, as opposed to its comorbidities?

options.text: Development of novel alpha-2-delta ligands specifically targeting PTSD hyperarousal
Expansion of SSRI prescribing to higher doses in PTSD
Psychotherapies, particularly exposure therapy, as the primary treatment for core PTSD symptoms
Use of long-acting benzodiazepines for sustained hyperarousal management
Use of mood stabilisers as adjuncts to SSRIs in PTSD

correct_answer.text: Psychotherapies, particularly exposure therapy, as the primary treatment for core PTSD symptoms

questions.explanation: The advance in treating PTSD has been divided — pharmacological treatments have improved management of comorbidities (depression, insomnia, pain, substance misuse), while psychotherapeutic approaches, particularly exposure therapy and various forms of CBT, have been the main advance for treating the core symptoms of PTSD. This highlights the essential complementary roles of pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy in comprehensive PTSD management.

questions.question_text: Rogerian therapy is the basis for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is an individualistic therapy that belongs to and is developed from Rogerian therapy principles, emphasizing client-centered, empathic approaches.

questions.question_text: Justin is a medical student who faints every time he encounters medical situations involving blood or injury. His therapist trains him to tense the muscles of the arms, legs, and torso at the earliest signs of faintness. This type of treatment is called
questions.explanation: This is called applied tension. Unlike those with other specifi c phobias who show an increase in sympathetic output on exposure to phobic stimuli, patients with blood–injury– injection phobia show a unique, biphasic response. The fi rst phase is associated with increased heart rate and blood pressure. In the second phase, however, the blood pressure suddenly falls and the patient faints. To treat the problem, patients are shown a series of slides that are provocative (e.g. mutilated bodies). They are trained to identify early-warning signs of fainting, such as queasiness, cold sweats, or dizziness. They also learn how to apply the learned muscle tension response quickly, contingent on these warning signs. Patients can also perform applied tension while donating blood or watching a surgical operation. The technique of isometric tension raises blood pressure, which prevents fainting. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 952.

questions.question_text: What is mentalization in psychology?

options.text: The ability to ignore others' mental states
The ability to understand the mental states of oneself or others that underlies overt behaviour
A form of dissociation from reality
A defense mechanism used in psychosis

correct_answer.text: The ability to understand the mental states of oneself or others that underlies overt behaviour

questions.explanation: Mentalization is the ability to understand the mental states of oneself or others that underlie overt behaviour, representing imaginative mental activity that allows perception and interpretation of human behaviour in terms of intentional mental states.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an alternative, effective treatment to dialectical behavioral therapy for severe borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation: MBT is a psychotherapy developed for the treatment of borderline personality disorder. It focuses on the mentalizing vulnerabilities of the patient in helping them to understand the attachment process.

questions.question_text: In family systems theory related to eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, which concept describes the process when a third person is introduced into a dyadic relationship to balance excessive intimacy, conflict, or distance?
questions.explanation: Triangulation (or triangling) is the process that occurs when a third person is introduced into a dyadic relationship to balance either excessive intimacy, conflict, or distance and provide stability in the system. In toxic relationships, it may involve manipulation and control.

questions.question_text: In Freud's model of mourning, what process must occur for healthy resolution of grief?

options.text: Full withdrawal of life force from attachment to the deceased (decathexis)

correct_answer.text: Full withdrawal of life force from attachment to the deceased (decathexis)

questions.explanation: Freud's model for mourning proposes that an individual's life force must be fully withdrawn from its attachment to the deceased person (decathexis).

questions.question_text: A therapist using Rogers' client-centered approach while incorporating Beck's cognitive model would most appropriately employ which therapeutic technique?
questions.explanation: When Rogerian person-centered principles are incorporated with Beck's cognitive model, the resulting approach is cognitive therapy, which combines the therapeutic relationship and acceptance of Rogers with the structured cognitive techniques of Beck.

questions.question_text: Rogerian therapy based on motivational interviewing is:
questions.explanation: Rogerian therapy (person-centered therapy developed by Carl Rogers) is based on humanistic principles and forms the foundation of motivational interviewing. It emphasizes unconditional positive regard, empathy, and self-actualization, contrasting with cognitive-behavioral or analytic approaches.

questions.question_text: Triangulation in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Involvement of a third party to reduce tension between two members

correct_answer.text: Involvement of a third party to reduce tension between two members

questions.explanation: Triangulation occurs when tension between two family members is managed by involving a third member, often an unhealthy family dynamic.

questions.question_text: A Rogerian psychotherapy developed by incorporating Beck's analytic therapy
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing evolved from Carl Rogers' person-centered therapy approach, incorporating elements of motivational psychology without rigidly adhering to Beck's cognitive therapy methodology.

questions.question_text: Jack has certain core beliefs about being unlovable. He thinks that this characteristic makes people abandon him. In order to avoid this, he turns out to be excessively self-sacrifi cing to his family. From a schema-based treatment point of view, what is the underlying cognitive process that is maintaining the schema?
questions.explanation: Schema-based approaches in cognitive therapy are based on the original ideas of Beck. Early life experiences produce a number of thought patterns or schemata. These thought patterns are like ‘block moulds’ into which thoughts fi t in when evaluating events. They are otherwise called core beliefs. These result in underlying ‘assumptions’ which reinforce the core beliefs and from these arise the negative automatic thoughts. Schemata are thought to be dormant, and get activated during a depressive episode. Schemata are patterns of unconditional beliefs that are hard to access and are self-maintaining. There are thought to be three main processes that maintain schemata. Schema surrender is the process where the person seeks evidence that supports the beliefs and dismisses any evidence to the contrary. Schema compensation refers to compensating for the core belief by doing the exact opposite, but, ultimately, this action acts as a reinforcer that maintains the schema, as in the case described in the question. Ultimately, the person believes that the family loves him only because he is self-sacrifi cing, and if he was not, he would still remain unlovable. Schema avoidance is a group of blocking behaviours that help avoid emotional arousal – e.g. comfort eating. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 149.

questions.question_text: Group therapy would be contraindicated for a patient in which of the following scenarios?

options.text: A new diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia with active delusions
A patient actively engaged in individual therapy, suffering from depression and suicidal thoughts
Bipolar disorder with manic symptoms has been diagnosed, though the patient is stable on medications
The patient has antisocial personality disorder and is with others in the group with the same diagnosis
The patient is suffering from an acute grief reaction after the death of a spouse

correct_answer.text: A new diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia with active delusions

questions.explanation: There are relatively few contraindications to participating in group therapy. A patient with active delusions, who incorporate the group into the delusions, and a patient who is threatening with frequent outbursts are some examples of patients who should be excluded from the group setting.

questions.question_text: Bowlby and Parkes' stage theory of grief includes all of the following stages EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Bowlby and Parkes proposed a 4-stage theory (Shock-numbness, Yearning-searching, Disorganization-despair, and Reorganization). Bargaining is a stage in Kübler-Ross's 5-stage model, not in Bowlby and Parkes' model.

questions.question_text: In substance abuse therapy, which approach uses alcohol or substance signifiers in controlled conditions to reduce cravings?
questions.explanation: Cue therapy, also known as cue exposure therapy, uses alcohol or substance signifiers in controlled conditions to help individuals with substance use disorders reduce their cravings and problematic behaviors related to substance abuse.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a Kleinian defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Isolation is not a Kleinian defence. It is characterized as a mental process involving the creation of a gap between an unpleasant cognition and other thoughts and feelings. The other defences (splitting, projective identification, introjection, denial) are more primitive and were addressed by Klein in her work with children. Kleinian defences are remembered by SIPDOG: Splitting, Introjection, Projection, Identification, Denial, Omnipotence, Grandiosity.

questions.question_text: Erich Lindemann's stages of grief include shock lasting approximately:
questions.explanation: According to Erich Lindemann's model, the shock stage of grief lasts approximately 10-14 days, followed by intense sadness, anger, and resolution within about a year.

questions.question_text: In the landmark National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program, which of the following psychotherapies was found to be equivalent to imipramine in severe depression?
questions.explanation: A landmark trial in the history of antidepressant psychotherapy was the multisite NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program. Investigators randomly assigned 250 outpatients with major depression to receive 16 weeks of IPT, CBT, imipramine plus clinical management, or placebo pills plus clinical management. This study was the fi rst comparison of IPT and CBT, each of which had demonstrated effi cacy in separate trials, and the fi rst trial to use treatment manuals and monitor the psychotherapeutic input of pharmacotherapists. Most patients completed at least 12 once-weekly treatment sessions or 15 weeks of therapy. Those with milder depression (defi ned as a score of <20 on the 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression) improved equally regardless of which treatment was used. For more severely depressed patients (those with a Ham-D score of 20), imipramine worked fastest and was most consistently superior to placebo. IPT and imipramine had comparable effects on Ham-D scores and several other outcome measures, and were superior to placebo for more severely depressed patients. CBT was not superior to placebo among the more depressed patients. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 300.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse treatment, people believe that they are helpless, hopeless and powerless
questions.explanation: The 12-step program acknowledges that individuals feel powerless over their addiction and emphasizes surrender to a higher power as part of recovery.

questions.question_text: Lisa is a 35-year-old lady, presenting with a diagnosis of depression. She has been referred by her psychiatrist for psychodynamic psychotherapy. According to her therapist, Lisa has the ability to conceive of her own mental state as explanations of her behaviour. This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: The capacity for mentalizing grows out of attachment theory and refers to a person’s ability to conceive of his or her own and others’ mental states as explanations of behaviour. Hence, it is related to psychological mindedness. The psychodynamic clinician assesses the ability of a patient to see that his or her behaviour grows out of a set of beliefs, feelings, and perspectives that are not necessarily the same as others’. Like empathy, mentalizing requires a capacity to sense what is going on in another’s mind and respond accordingly. This capacity to be sensitive to what others are feeling and to know that one’s internal states contribute to one’s behaviour augurs well for a more exploratory or interpretative approach in dynamic psychotherapy. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry,1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p 29.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is the central principle of dualsex treatment as developed by Masters and Johnson?

options.text: This shows your pattern of seeing me as untrustworthy.
You seem to be testing whether I will set appropriate boundaries.
Let's explore what this might mean in the context of your experience.

questions.explanation: Several synthetic and semisynthetic opioids are not detected on routine urine toxicology screening. For instance, fentanyl, buprenorphine, and methadone require assays for these substances in particular given structural differences relative to naturally occurring opioids (i.e., opiates), including morphine and codeine. Of note, all agents that activate mu receptors are known as opioids (literally, “resembling opiates”), and agonists that are structurally related to compounds derived from opium poppy are opiates proper. The DSM5 uses the more encompassing term opioid, as in “opioid use disorder” and “opioid withdrawal.”

questions.question_text: A woman comes to your outpatient clinic. She has recurrent thoughts of contamination with germs and has to wash her hands up to 20 times every time she touches wooden surfaces. This prevents her from looking after her 2-year-old child. She is worried that the child may not be gaining the required weight. She has also started to lose the skin of her palms due to the excessive washing. The treatment you would recommend would be

options.text: Combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and CBT

correct_answer.text: Combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and CBT

questions.explanation: According to NICE guidelines, in the initial treatment of adults with OCD, low-intensity psychological treatments (including exposure and response prevention (ERP)) (up to 10 therapist hours per patient) should be offered if the patient’s degree of functional impairment is mild and/ or the patient expresses a preference for a low-intensity approach. These include brief individual CBT (including ERP) using structured self-help materials; brief individual CBT (including ERP) by telephone; group CBT (including ERP) (note, the patient may receive more than 10 hours of therapy in this format). Those with mild functional impairment who are unable to engage in low intensity CBT (including ERP), or for whom low-intensity treatment has proved to be inadequate, should be offered the choice of either a course of an SSRI or more intensive CBT (including ERP) (more than 10 therapist hours per patient). Adults with OCD with moderate functional impairment should be offered the choice of either a course of an SSRI or more intensive CBT (including ERP) (more than 10 therapist hours per patient). Adults with OCD with severe functional impairment should be offered combined treatment with an SSRI and CBT (including ERP). NICE. CG31 Obsessive-compulsive disorder: NICE guideline. Clinical Guidelines (accessed 7 June 7 2009 http://guidance.nice.org.uk/CG31/NiceGuidance/pdf/English).

questions.question_text: In the context of treating addiction, which therapy uses Rogers's method while incorporating Beck's cognitive behaviour model?
questions.explanation: When a question asks about Rogerian approach incorporating Beck's cognitive behaviour model, cognitive therapy is the appropriate answer that combines these approaches.

questions.question_text: During a biofeedback session, which of the following denotes a stage of relaxation?

options.text: Dominance of alpha waves on EEG recording
Decrease in muscle tension on electromyogram (EMG)

questions.explanation: Biofeedback is the process where certain physiological parameters of an individual are recorded and displayed. It is usually used in combination with relaxation. This involves the recording of small changes in the physiological levels (induced by relaxation) of the feedback parameter. The display can be visual or auditory. Patients are instructed to change the levels of the physiological parameter, using the feedback from the display. It is based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning. The feedback instrument used depends on the patient and the specifi c problem. The most effective instruments are the electromyogram (EMG), which measures the electrical potentials of muscle fi bres; the electroencephalogram (EEG), which measures alpha waves that occur in relaxed states; the galvanic skin response (GSR) gauge, which shows decreased skin conductivity during a relaxed state; and the thermistor, which measures skin temperature (which drops during tension because of peripheral vasoconstriction). For example, in the treatment of bruxism, an EMG electrode is attached to the masseter muscle. The EMG emits a loud tone when the muscle is contracted and a low tone when at rest. Patients can learn to alter the tone to indicate relaxation. Patients receive feedback about the masseter muscle, the tone reinforces the learning, and the condition ameliorates. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 950.

questions.question_text: Structural Family Therapy A therapist focuses on changing unspoken rules, boundaries, and hierarchies within a family. Which type of therapy is this?
questions.explanation: Structural family therapy (Minuchin) focuses on family structure, boundaries, hierarchies, and subsystems.

questions.question_text: Cognitive treatment aims to modify the schemas that perpetuate depression or anxiety. Which of the following is least likely with respect to schemas?

options.text: Schemas act as cognitive frameworks that filter and interpret incoming information
Schemas are behaviours representative of the individual’s presenting problem
Conditional assumptions and rules can operate as dysfunctional schemas
Schemas represent fundamental beliefs and assumptions about the self
Not all schemas are pathological or contribute to psychological distress

correct_answer.text: Schemas are behaviours representative of the individual’s presenting problem

questions.explanation: Schemas determine our perceptions, assimilations, and actions upon the externally received information. These are developed through early experiences in childhood and formative infl uences thereafter. According to Beck, these are deeper cognitive structures than the negative automatic thoughts that are readily observable in clients undergoing cognitive behavioural therapy. Everyone interacts with the external world by utilizing his/her set of schemas. Most of these are simple schemas that do not contribute to any psychopathology. So schemas are conditional rules (‘if–then statements’) while the others are core beliefs about oneself (‘I am good-looking’, ‘I cannot write a poem’, etc). Clients requiring CBT often have a cluster of maladaptive schemas that perpetuate depression or anxiety state. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2004. p. 2516.

questions.question_text: In family systems theory, family members ganging up against one family member describes
questions.explanation: Detouring (or scapegoating) occurs when parents form an alliance against a child, focusing negativity on the child to distract from tension in their marital relationship. This creates distance between the parents and the child while increasing parental closeness.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach combines Rogerian method with Beck's cognitive behaviour model?
questions.explanation: Cognitive therapy represents the incorporation of Rogerian principles with Beck's cognitive behaviour model. Motivational interviewing is based on Rogerian principles alone, while cue exposure therapy is used specifically for addiction management in protective environments.

questions.question_text: In substance abuse treatment, a therapeutic approach that addresses beliefs that individuals are helpless, hopeless, and powerless is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The 12-step program framework addresses beliefs of helplessness, hopelessness, and powerlessness by introducing the concept of surrendering to a higher power and finding support through group participation and spiritual growth.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes mentalization?

options.text: A process of imaginative mental activity that allows perception and interpretation of human behavior in terms of intentional mental states
A state of increased awareness of one's physical sensations
The ability to construct personal theories about oneself
A technique for improving attention and focus
The capacity to predict future behaviors based on past patterns

correct_answer.text: A process of imaginative mental activity that allows perception and interpretation of human behavior in terms of intentional mental states

questions.explanation: Mentalization is defined as a form of imaginative mental activity that enables individuals to perceive and interpret human behavior in terms of intentional mental states, primarily concerning the reflection of affective (emotional) mental states.

questions.question_text: Paradoxical Injunction A family therapist instructs the family to continue their dysfunctional pattern of interaction. Which type of family therapy uses paradoxical injunction?
questions.explanation: Paradoxical injunction (prescribing the symptom) is a systemic/Milan family therapy technique.

questions.question_text: Caution should be used in conducting hypnosis on a patient with which of the following characteristics?
questions.explanation: Negative emotions can surface in patients with poor reality testing. As a result, caution should be used in performing hypnosis in those with paranoia, or a high need for control.

questions.question_text: During a CBT session, a patient says I'm terrible at my job; I made a mistake yesterday. The therapist responds: Why don't we see this as an opportunity to learn rather than evidence you're terrible? Which CBT technique is the therapist using?
questions.explanation: Reframing restructures negative interpretations into alternative, more adaptive perspectives.

questions.question_text: A patient expressing, “cabbages to kings” during a therapy session is a good example of which fundamental technique in psychoanalysis?
questions.explanation: Free association is a predominant technique in psychoanalysis. The fundamental rule of free association is for the patient to tell the analysis everything that comes to their mind, the unimportant and nonsensical, and it does not mirror normal conversation.

questions.question_text: Focusing on a detail out of context while ignoring other, more salient features in the situation is called
questions.explanation: The statement refers to selective abstraction, one of the cognitive biases seen in depression. Other cognitive biases include arbitrary inference, drawing a specifi c conclusion in the absence of evidence or when the evidence is contrary to the conclusion; overgeneralization, drawing a conclusion on the basis of one or more isolated incidents; dichotomous thinking, the tendency to classify experience in one of two extreme categories, ignoring more moderate variations; personalization, the tendency to relate external events to oneself; magnifi cation/ minimization,- exaggerating (i.e. catastrophizing) or belittling the signifi cance or magnitude of an event. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 173.

questions.question_text: Reciprocal communication in therapeutic settings most directly enhances which element of the therapeutic relationship?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal communication is fundamental to establishing rapport, the working alliance between therapist and patient.

questions.question_text: Rogerian therapy combined with Beck's cognitive techniques describes which therapeutic approach?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing integrates Rogerian person-centered principles (empathy, acceptance) with cognitive techniques to enhance motivation for change.

questions.question_text: A colleague on your team states they no longer wish to contact a patient because the patient makes threats of self-harm at the end of calls. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Send a boundary-setting letter to the patient
Advise the colleague to improve their self-care before continuing contact
Discuss countertransference with the team to understand what the patient is communicating
Flag the case to social work immediately
Exclude the patient from future appointments

correct_answer.text: Discuss countertransference with the team to understand what the patient is communicating

questions.explanation: The appropriate response is to explore the countertransference within the team, as the patient's behavior (self-harm threats) may be communicating distress and the team's reaction to it provides valuable clinical information about the therapeutic relationship.

questions.question_text: In a therapeutic community, the members tolerate behaviour that may not be accepted anywhere else. This process is called
questions.explanation: Permissiveness is the principle where members tolerate behaviour that they may not accept elsewhere. This is also helped by the members having the opportunity to be helpful to others through both cognitive understanding and emotional linking (imparting information, providing feedback, and altruism). Mutual help is the process by which members support each other and help each other to change. Imitation is the conscious emulation of one’s behaviour following that of another – also called role modelling. Altruism is the process of putting another person’s need ahead of one’s own and in the process learning there is value in giving to others. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 608. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 937.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach combines Rogers' person-centered principles with Beck's cognitive techniques?
questions.explanation: Cognitive therapy, developed by Beck, incorporates structured goal-oriented techniques while the combination with Rogerian principles emphasizes the therapeutic relationship and client autonomy in recognizing and modifying unhelpful thinking patterns.

questions.question_text: What therapy involves creating an anxiety hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization involves creating an anxiety hierarchy and gradual exposure to feared stimuli paired with relaxation techniques (reciprocal inhibition).

questions.question_text: According to Bowlby and Parkes' stage theory of grief, which of the following is NOT one of the four stages?
questions.explanation: Bowlby and Parkes' four-stage theory of grief (SYDR) includes shock-numbness, yearning-searching, disorganization-despair, and reorganization, but does not include bargaining as a separate stage.

questions.question_text: Nick has been presenting with a diagnosis of major depression. His GP is considering referring Nick for psychodynamic psychotherapy. According to the GP, Nick has certain qualities he thinks are significant for a good clinical outlook in psychodynamic psychotherapy. Which of the qualities shown by Nick has been shown NOT to predict good response in psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: High levels of personality pathology or severe personality traits

questions.explanation: Most psychotherapists consider certain qualities in their patients as prerequisites for engaging in psychodynamic psychotherapy. These include psychological mindedness: curiosity about oneself and the capacity for self-scrutiny. Those who are unable to articulate and comprehend their inner thoughts and feelings cannot negotiate with the fundamental analytical words and their meanings. The inability to examine one’s own motivations and behaviours precludes benefi ts from the analytical method. Introspectiveness: the person should be able to experience and learn from intense affects or confl icts without acting them out. The person should be able to form reasonable object relationships, usually the capacity to form and maintain, as well as to detach from, a trusting object relationship is essential. High motivation: the patient needs a strong motivation to persevere, in light of the rigors of intense and lengthy treatment. The desire for health and self-understanding must surpass the neurotic need for unhappiness. The person should be able to tolerate frustration and therapeutic regression. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 926. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1862.

questions.question_text: Which skill is considered the first step in effective interpersonal problem solving?
questions.explanation: Acquiring good social perception is considered the first step in effective interpersonal problem solving. Training someone to perceive and interpret social and cognitive cues can help with more specific communication and coping skills.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is a technique for automatic thought modifi cation?

options.text: Behavioral activation and scheduling of pleasant activities

questions.explanation: Examining the evidence is a technique in which the therapist and patient collaboratively explore the evidence for and the evidence against a specifi c distorted thought or belief. When working through the exercise, the therapist asks the patient to write the thought or belief at the top of a piece of paper and then label two columns with ‘evidence for’ and ‘evidence against’ the thought. The patient is then guided to explore methodically and write down each piece of evidence. At the end of this procedure, the evidence for and against the cognition is quantifi ed and estimated. Guided discovery is the most frequently used technique to help patients articulate automatic thoughts in sessions. The specifi c technique used is called Socratic questioning. One of the most powerful ways of teaching patients to detect automatic thoughts is to fi nd a real-life example of how automatic thoughts infl uence their emotional responses. A shift in mood during the therapy session can be an opportune time for the therapist to facilitate the identifi cation of automatic thoughts. The Automatic Thoughts Questionnaire devised by Hollon and Kendall is a comprehensive list of dysfunctional thoughts that has been used primarily in research studies. Similar lists can be used in clinical settings when patients are having diffi culty detecting their automatic thoughts. Imagery and role-play are two methods for uncovering cognitions when direct questions are unsuccessful (or partially successful) in generating suspected automatic thinking. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 208. Hollon SD and Kendall PC (1980) Cognitive self-statements in depression: development of an automatic thoughts questionnaire. Cognitive Therapy and Research 4: 383–395.

questions.question_text: A therapist says to a patient: We had a heated discussion last session. I've tried to discuss it several times today, but you're avoiding it. Shall we talk about it now? Which therapeutic technique is being employed?
questions.explanation: Confrontation addresses avoidance or discrepancies, bringing them into the patient's awareness.

questions.question_text: During her fi rst session, Lisa asks her therapist about certain terms she came across on the internet. “What is transference?”

options.text: A learned response pattern that the individual applies to the therapist
Therapist’s response to the individual based on the therapist’s previous relationships
individual’s response to the therapist based on the individual’s previous relationships
Transfer of positive thoughts from the therapist to the individual through self-disclosure

correct_answer.text: individual’s response to the therapist based on the individual’s previous relationships

questions.explanation: Transference is the displacement of feelings and thoughts associated with a fi gure in the patient’s past onto the therapist. Transference is often unconscious, at least initially, and the patient is often puzzled by their behaviour towards the therapist because it does not make sense, based on who the therapist really is. Hence the enactment of missing a session or of coming late to a session may reveal unconscious transference. The prevailing view about transference is that the therapist’s actual behaviour always infl uences the patient’s experience of the therapist. Hence the transference to the therapist is partly based on real characteristics and partly on fi gures from the patient’s past: a combination of old and new relationships. Many therapists believe that interpretation of this transference is an essential process of psychodynamic psychotherapy. Gabbard says that one should postpone the interpretation of transference until it becomes a resistance and until it is close to the patient’s awareness. In other words, if things are going reasonably well, it makes no sense to interpret transference. If the patient develops, for example, erotized or highly negative feelings, which impede the process of the therapy, interpretation may be essential. Many therapists regard treatment that focuses on transference as more exploratory than therapy geared to extra-transference relationships. In supportive therapy, interpretation of the transference may be minimized, although the therapist may silently interpret the transference as a way of increasing his or her understanding of the patient. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 56. Tasman A, Maj M, First M B, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1854.

questions.question_text: A patient being treated for anxiety and depression tells the therapist about how embarrassed she was in forgetting the words for her class presentation today and states that she knows she will never make it as a teacher in the future. This is an example of which of the following cognitive distortions?
questions.explanation: Cognitive distortions, also known as automatic thoughts, are the thoughts that occur between external events and a person’s emotional reaction to the event. The vignette above is an example of overgeneralization in which an overwhelmingly negative conclusion is drawn from a relatively minor event.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which correctly describes counter-transference?

options.text: The analyst’s or psychotherapist’s transference reactions to the individual
His or her reactions to the individual’s transferences
Any reactions, feelings and attitudes of the analyst or therapist towards the individual, regardless of their source.

questions.explanation: Freud used the term counter-transference to describe the analyst’s transference towards the patient. In other words, the patient might remind the therapist of someone from the therapist’s past, so that the therapist starts to treat the patient as though he or she were that fi gure. Over time, this view of counter-transference was broadened to include the total emotional reaction of the therapist to the patient. Today it is recognized that counter- transference is jointly created—it partly involves the therapist’s past relationships, but it also involves feelings induced in the therapist by the patient’s behaviour. Counter-transference is variously defi ned as (1) the analyst’s or psychotherapist’s transference reactions to the patient; (2) his or her reactions to the patient’s transferences; and (3) any reactions, feelings and attitudes of the analyst or therapist toward the patient, regardless of their source. These responses are manifestations of the requisite engagement by the therapist or analyst in the emotional process of treatment. Moreover, these reactions are a rich source of understanding of the patient’s experience as it touches the therapist affectively. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 58. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1854.

questions.question_text: Rogerian therapy is based on which therapeutic principle?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is an individualistic therapy that belongs to the Rogerian tradition. It emphasizes the therapeutic alliance and client-centered approach consistent with Carl Rogers' principles of unconditional positive regard and congruence.

questions.question_text: A therapist says: You mentioned your mother is always going out and comes back late, never at home. What do you think she does when she goes out? Which therapeutic technique is being used?
questions.explanation: Clarification seeks to understand and make vague or ambiguous statements more precise.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse therapy, alcohol or substance signifier is used in controlled conditions
questions.explanation: Cue-based therapy uses alcohol or substance-related cues (signifiers) presented in controlled, safe environments to facilitate extinction of conditioned responses and reduce cravings.

questions.question_text: Which intervention specifically focuses on enabling the patient to express personal reasons for and against improving their treatment adherence?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing enables the patient to express personal reasons for and against improving their treatment adherence.

questions.question_text: Which intervention specifically uses analogies with chronic physical illness to explore the pros and cons of medication?
questions.explanation: In compliance therapy, a patient’s ambivalence towards medication is explored, analogies with chronic physical illness are made, and the pros and cons of medication are considered during the course of treatment.

questions.question_text: Which element is most important in CBT for psychosis?

options.text: Symptom reduction as the sole goal
Challenging false beliefs early in treatment

questions.explanation: In CBT for psychosis, establishing a strong therapeutic alliance and developing a shared formulation of the psychotic symptoms is essential before challenging beliefs; premature confrontation can rupture the alliance.

questions.question_text: What is the role the therapist should play in working with a patient for psychiatric rehabilitation?

options.text: To act as a parental figure
To be a shared decision maker
To make medical appointments for the patient
To suggest a variety of potential jobs for the patient
To take a stance on the patient not using alcohol or drugs

correct_answer.text: To be a shared decision maker

questions.explanation: The practitioner’s role is to be in a partnership with the patient to help improve their quality of life and collaborate with them and to work as a shared decision maker, rather than a parental or authority figure.

questions.question_text: A form of therapy where patients admit to feelings of helplessness and powerlessness is best described as:
questions.explanation: Cognitive-behavioral therapy addresses learned helplessness by helping patients recognize their sense of powerlessness and develop adaptive coping strategies.

questions.question_text: Reflecting on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviors is characteristic of which therapeutic approach?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing helps people explore ambivalence and find internal motivation for change by examining the relationship between current behaviors and desired outcomes.

questions.question_text: Which type of therapy asks patients to direct their attention to specific body area while thinking certain phrases reflecting a relaxed state, progressing through various themes including cardiac regulation and breathing adjustment?
questions.explanation: Autogenic training can help with relaxation by having the patient direct attention to specific body areas and think phrases to help them relax (i.e., My forehead is cool.).

questions.question_text: The process by which unconscious ideas are repressed and prevented from reaching awareness because they are unacceptable in psychotherapy is called
questions.explanation: Resistance is broadly defined as the conscious or, more often, unconscious force within the patient opposing the emergence of unconscious material. Resistance is thought of as the patient’s attempt to protect her or himself by avoiding the anticipated emotional discomfort that accompanies the emergence of conflictual, dangerous, or painful experiences, feelings, thoughts, memories, needs, and desires. Resistance occurs through the use of unconscious defence mechanisms. The recognition, clarification, and interpretation of resistance constitute important activities of the psychoanalyst and the psychoanalytic psychotherapist, both of whom must first appreciate how a patient is warding off anxiety before understanding why he or she is so compelled. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 926.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which in the least likely outcome in a individual undergoing CBT for hypochondriasis?

options.text: Less distress at thoughts of illness
A diagnosis of decrease in health-related anxiety

questions.explanation: In a 12-month follow-up randomized controlled trial of CBT vs treatment as usual, CBT was found to be better than medical care as usual. Compared with the control group, the CBT group had signifi cantly lower levels of hypochondriacal symptoms, beliefs, and attitudes and health-related anxiety at 12 months. They also had less impairment of social role functioning and intermediate activities of daily living. However, hypochondriacal somatic symptoms did not improve signifi cantly. The authors of the study Barsky and Ahern explained, ‘Conceptually, hypochondriacal somatic symptoms cannot simply be stripped away with symptomatic treatment, because they exist for underlying psychological and interpersonal reasons. This suggests that a realistic goal in treating hypochondriasis is amelioration of distressing fears and beliefs and improved coping, rather than the elimination of somatic symptoms per se.’ Barsky AJ and Ahern DK. Cognitive behavior therapy for hypochondriasis: a randomized, controlled trial. Journal of the American Medical Association 2004; 291: 1464–1470.

questions.question_text: The term 'Dream Work' described by Sigmund Freud involves 

options.text: Multiple images in dreams represent one unconscious impulse
Transforming latent content into manifest content
Transfer of energy from an original object to a symbolic representation of the object

correct_answer.text: Transforming latent content into manifest content

questions.explanation: Freud distinguished two types/layers of dream content. Manifest Content refers to what is recalled by the dreamer; Latent Content refers to unconscious thoughts and wishes that threaten to awaken the dreamer. The unconscious mental operation by which the Latent Content is transformed into Manifest Content is called the Dream Work.

questions.question_text: You are the junior doctor at a unit for severe personality disordered patients, otherwise known as a therapeutic community. You observe group therapy and attempt to identify group dynamics based on what you have read in theory? Which of the following best describes 'group cohesion'?

options.text: When the group works together towards a common goal
The process by which mere expression of ideas and conflicts is accompanied by an emotional response which produces a
The quality of the relationship that develops between each individual member and the therapist
When an individual incorporates the characteristics and qualities of the group

correct_answer.text: When the group works together towards a common goal
